cases.title: Dividing two integers

spark.statement: SELECT a / b AS q FROM t ORDER BY a DESC
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL built-in functions: expr1 / expr2 always performs floating point division.

databricks.statement: SELECT a / b AS q FROM t ORDER BY a DESC
databricks.source: Databricks SQL / (slash sign) operator: DOUBLE unless both sides are DECIMAL or intervals.

snowflake.statement: SELECT a / b AS q FROM t ORDER BY a DESC
snowflake.source: Snowflake arithmetic operators: division scale is max(S1, min(S1 + 6, 12)).
snowflake.note: Scale 6 is documented. That precision stops at 38 for NUMBER(38,0) operands is assumed.

tsql.statement: SELECT a / b AS q FROM t ORDER BY a DESC
tsql.source: T-SQL / (Divide): an integer divided by an integer is an integer, the fraction truncated.

duckdb.statement: SELECT a / b AS q FROM t ORDER BY a DESC
duckdb.source: DuckDB numeric operators: / is floating-point division, // is integer division.

cases.title: Dividing two DECIMAL(10,2) values

spark.statement: SELECT d1 / d2 AS q FROM t
spark.source: Spark's DecimalPrecision rule: scale max(6, s1 + p2 + 1), precision p1 - s1 + s2 + scale.
spark.note: The rule is in Spark's source; the SQL reference doesn't state it.

databricks.statement: SELECT d1 / d2 AS q FROM t
databricks.source: Databricks SQL / (slash sign) operator: DECIMAL when both sides are DECIMAL.
databricks.note: The page says DECIMAL without the precision and scale.

snowflake.statement: SELECT d1 / d2 AS q FROM t
snowflake.source: Snowflake arithmetic operators: L = L1 + S2, S = max(S1, min(S1 + 6, 12)), P = L + S, rounded.

tsql.statement: SELECT d1 / d2 AS q FROM t
tsql.source: T-SQL precision, scale and length: e1 / e2 has precision p1 - s1 + s2 + max(6, s1 + p2 + 1) and scale max(6, s1 + p2 + 1).

duckdb.statement: SELECT d1 / d2 AS q FROM t
duckdb.source: DuckDB numeric operators: / is floating-point division.

cases.title: Where NULL sorts in ascending order

spark.statement: SELECT v FROM t ORDER BY v
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL ORDER BY clause: NULLS FIRST is the default for ascending order.

databricks.statement: SELECT v FROM t ORDER BY v
databricks.source: Databricks SQL ORDER BY clause: NULLS FIRST is the default for ascending order.

snowflake.statement: SELECT v FROM t ORDER BY v
snowflake.source: Snowflake ORDER BY: NULL values are higher than any other value, so ascending order returns them last.

tsql.statement: SELECT v FROM t ORDER BY v
tsql.source: T-SQL ORDER BY clause: NULL values are treated as the lowest possible values.

duckdb.statement: SELECT v FROM t ORDER BY v
duckdb.source: DuckDB ORDER BY clause: NULLS LAST is the default.

cases.title: COUNT and SUM over a column with a NULL

spark.statement: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, COUNT(v) AS nv, SUM(v) AS s FROM t
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL built-in functions count and sum.
spark.note: The values are documented. The BIGINT types are not stated in Spark's reference.

databricks.statement: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, COUNT(v) AS nv, SUM(v) AS s FROM t
databricks.source: Databricks SQL count (BIGINT, NULLs not counted) and sum (BIGINT for integral input).

snowflake.statement: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, COUNT(v) AS nv, SUM(v) AS s FROM t
snowflake.source: Snowflake COUNT and SUM: NULL values are ignored.

tsql.statement: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, COUNT(v) AS nv, SUM(v) AS s FROM t
tsql.source: T-SQL COUNT returns int. SUM of int returns int. Both ignore NULL values.

duckdb.statement: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, COUNT(v) AS nv, SUM(v) AS s FROM t
duckdb.source: DuckDB aggregate functions: count is BIGINT, sum of INTEGER is HUGEINT.
duckdb.note: HUGEINT reaches Arrow as DECIMAL(38,0), which integer_width accepts.

cases.title: Joining a string with NULL

spark.statement: SELECT concat(s1, s2) AS c, s1 || s2 AS p FROM t
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL built-in functions concat and ||.
spark.note: The reference doesn't say what a NULL argument gives.

databricks.statement: SELECT concat(s1, s2) AS c, s1 || s2 AS p FROM t
databricks.source: Databricks SQL concat, a synonym for ||.
databricks.note: The page doesn't say what a NULL argument gives.

snowflake.statement: SELECT CONCAT(s1, s2) AS c, s1 || s2 AS p FROM t
snowflake.source: Snowflake CONCAT and ||: if any argument is NULL, the result is NULL.

tsql.statement: SELECT CONCAT(s1, s2) AS c, s1 + s2 AS p FROM t
tsql.source: T-SQL CONCAT turns NULL into an empty string. + with a NULL gives NULL (CONCAT_NULL_YIELDS_NULL is on).

duckdb.statement: SELECT concat(s1, s2) AS c, s1 || s2 AS p FROM t
duckdb.source: DuckDB text functions: concat skips NULL arguments, || gives NULL.

cases.title: Truncating a timestamp to its month

spark.statement: SELECT date_trunc('MONTH', ts) AS m FROM t
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL built-in functions date_trunc.
spark.note: The value is documented. The type for a TIMESTAMP_NTZ input isn't stated.

databricks.statement: SELECT date_trunc('MONTH', ts) AS m FROM t
databricks.source: Databricks SQL date_trunc returns a TIMESTAMP.
databricks.note: The page doesn't name TIMESTAMP_NTZ input, so the type here isn't confirmed.

snowflake.statement: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('MONTH', ts) AS m FROM t
snowflake.source: Snowflake DATE_TRUNC returns a value of the same type as its input.

tsql.statement: SELECT DATETRUNC(month, ts) AS m FROM t
tsql.source: T-SQL DATETRUNC returns the same type as its date argument.

duckdb.statement: SELECT date_trunc('month', ts) AS m FROM t
duckdb.source: DuckDB timestamp functions: date_trunc of a TIMESTAMP is a TIMESTAMP.

cases.title: A timestamp without a time zone keeps its wall-clock time

spark.statement: SELECT CAST('2024-03-10 02:30:00' AS TIMESTAMP_NTZ) AS ts FROM t
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL data types: TIMESTAMP_NTZ is a timestamp without time zone.

databricks.statement: SELECT CAST('2024-03-10 02:30:00' AS TIMESTAMP_NTZ) AS ts FROM t
databricks.source: Databricks SQL TIMESTAMP_NTZ type: no time zone is applied.

snowflake.statement: SELECT '2024-03-10 02:30:00'::TIMESTAMP_NTZ AS ts FROM t
snowflake.source: Snowflake TIMESTAMP_NTZ: wall-clock time, no time zone taken into account.

tsql.statement: SELECT CAST('2024-03-10 02:30:00' AS datetime2) AS ts FROM t
tsql.source: T-SQL datetime2 has no time zone.

duckdb.statement: SELECT CAST('2024-03-10 02:30:00' AS TIMESTAMP) AS ts FROM t
duckdb.source: DuckDB TIMESTAMP is a timestamp without time zone.

cases.title: COALESCE, a two-way IF and CASE with a NULL

duckdb.statement: SELECT COALESCE(a, 0) AS c, CASE WHEN a > 1 THEN 'big' ELSE 'small' END AS k, if(a > 1, 1, 0) AS f FROM t ORDER BY id
duckdb.source: DuckDB conditional functions coalesce and if, and CASE.

cases.note: T-SQL has no boolean values in a select list, so it has no statement here.

spark.statement: SELECT b1 AND b2 AS a, b1 OR b2 AS o, NOT b2 AS n FROM t ORDER BY id
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL NULL semantics: logical operators follow three-valued logic.

databricks.statement: SELECT b1 AND b2 AS a, b1 OR b2 AS o, NOT b2 AS n FROM t ORDER BY id
databricks.source: Databricks SQL NULL semantics: logical operators follow three-valued logic.

snowflake.statement: SELECT b1 AND b2 AS a, b1 OR b2 AS o, NOT b2 AS n FROM t ORDER BY id
snowflake.source: Snowflake ternary logic.

cases.title: SUBSTRING with a negative, zero and out-of-range start

spark.statement: SELECT substr(s, 5, 1) AS a, substr(s, -3, 3) AS b, substr(s, 0, 3) AS c, substr(s, -10, 5) AS d FROM t
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL built-in functions: substr, pos is 1-based; substr('Spark SQL', -3) is SQL, substr('Spark SQL', 5, 1) is k.
spark.note: Spark's reference doesn't say what a start of 0 or a start before the string's first character gives. Spa (0 read as 1) is from Spark's source (UTF8String.substringSQL); Spar is the answer Databricks documents for FROM -10 FOR 5.

databricks.statement: SELECT substr(s, 5, 1) AS a, substr(s, -3, 3) AS b, substr(s, 0, 3) AS c, substr(s, -10, 5) AS d FROM t
databricks.source: Databricks SQL substring function: pos is 1-based, a negative pos counts from the end; substring('Spark SQL' FROM -10 FOR 5) is Spar.
databricks.note: The page doesn't say what a start of 0 gives. Spa (0 read as 1) is from Spark's source.

snowflake.statement: SELECT SUBSTR(s, 5, 1) AS a, SUBSTR(s, -3, 3) AS b, SUBSTR(s, 0, 3) AS c, SUBSTR(s, -10, 5) AS d FROM t
snowflake.source: Snowflake SUBSTR, SUBSTRING: start is 1-based, 0 is treated as 1, a negative start counts from the end, and a position outside the string gives an empty value.

tsql.statement: SELECT SUBSTRING(s, 5, 1) AS a, SUBSTRING(s, -3, 3) AS b, SUBSTRING(s, 0, 3) AS c, SUBSTRING(s, -10, 5) AS d FROM t
tsql.source: T-SQL SUBSTRING: if start is less than 1, the result begins at the first character and has the larger of start + length - 1 and 0 characters.

duckdb.statement: SELECT substring(s, 5, 1) AS a, substring(s, -3, 3) AS b, substring(s, 0, 3) AS c, substring(s, -10, 5) AS d FROM t
duckdb.source: DuckDB text functions: substring, a start of 1 is the first character.
duckdb.note: DuckDB's page doesn't say what a start of 0 or a negative start gives. The expectation follows the SQL standard's SUBSTRING (the characters at positions start to start + length - 1 that exist).

cases.title: Character length, trailing spaces and byte length

spark.statement: SELECT id, length(s) AS n_chars, octet_length(s) AS n_bytes FROM t ORDER BY id
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL built-in functions: length is the character length and includes trailing spaces; octet_length is the byte length.

databricks.statement: SELECT id, length(s) AS n_chars, octet_length(s) AS n_bytes FROM t ORDER BY id
databricks.source: Databricks SQL length (character length, trailing spaces included) and octet_length (byte length) functions.

snowflake.statement: SELECT id, LENGTH(s) AS n_chars, OCTET_LENGTH(s) AS n_bytes FROM t ORDER BY id
snowflake.source: Snowflake LENGTH: the number of characters, a UTF-8 character counts once (Joyeux Noël is 11). OCTET_LENGTH: the length in bytes.

tsql.statement: SELECT id, LEN(s) AS n_chars, DATALENGTH(s) AS n_bytes FROM t ORDER BY id
tsql.source: T-SQL LEN excludes trailing spaces; DATALENGTH is the size in bytes and doesn't trim. Fabric Warehouse collation: varchar is UTF-8 (Latin1_General_100_BIN2_UTF8).
tsql.note: 5 bytes for Noël assumes a UTF-8 varchar column, the Fabric Warehouse default.

duckdb.statement: SELECT id, length(s) AS n_chars, strlen(s) AS n_bytes FROM t ORDER BY id
duckdb.source: DuckDB text functions: length is the number of characters, strlen the number of bytes.

cases.title: TRIM, UPPER, LOWER and a case-sensitive REPLACE

spark.statement: SELECT trim(s) AS tr, upper(s) AS up, lower(s) AS lo, replace(s, 'b', 'x') AS re FROM t
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL built-in functions trim, upper, lower and replace (replace('ABCabc', 'abc', 'DEF') is ABCDEF).

databricks.statement: SELECT trim(s) AS tr, upper(s) AS up, lower(s) AS lo, replace(s, 'b', 'x') AS re FROM t
databricks.source: Databricks SQL trim, upper, lower and replace functions.
databricks.note: Under the default UTF8_BINARY collation replace is case-sensitive; the replace page doesn't say so.

snowflake.statement: SELECT TRIM(s) AS tr, UPPER(s) AS up, LOWER(s) AS lo, REPLACE(s, 'b', 'x') AS re FROM t
snowflake.source: Snowflake TRIM, UPPER, LOWER and REPLACE.
snowflake.note: The REPLACE page doesn't say whether matching is case-sensitive.

tsql.statement: SELECT TRIM(s) AS tr, UPPER(s) AS up, LOWER(s) AS lo, REPLACE(s, 'b', 'x') AS re FROM t
tsql.source: T-SQL TRIM, UPPER, LOWER and REPLACE (comparisons follow the input's collation); Fabric Warehouse collation Latin1_General_100_BIN2_UTF8 is case-sensitive.

duckdb.statement: SELECT trim(s) AS tr, upper(s) AS up, lower(s) AS lo, replace(s, 'b', 'x') AS re FROM t
duckdb.source: DuckDB text functions trim, upper, lower and replace.
duckdb.note: The page doesn't say whether replace matches case-sensitively.

cases.title: Whether LIKE matches case-sensitively

spark.statement: SELECT id, CASE WHEN s LIKE 'a%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS m FROM t ORDER BY id
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL built-in functions: like matches the pattern literally; ilike matches case-insensitively.

databricks.statement: SELECT id, CASE WHEN s LIKE 'a%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS m FROM t ORDER BY id
databricks.source: Databricks SQL like operator.
databricks.note: The page doesn't say whether matching is case-sensitive; the default collation UTF8_BINARY suggests it is.

snowflake.statement: SELECT id, CASE WHEN s LIKE 'a%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS m FROM t ORDER BY id
snowflake.source: Snowflake [ NOT ] LIKE: performs a case-sensitive comparison; use ILIKE for case-insensitive matching.

tsql.statement: SELECT id, CASE WHEN s LIKE 'a%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS m FROM t ORDER BY id
tsql.source: T-SQL LIKE follows the collation; Fabric Warehouse collation: the default Latin1_General_100_BIN2_UTF8 is case-sensitive.
tsql.note: SQL Server's usual default collation is case-insensitive, where row 1 would match too.

duckdb.statement: SELECT id, CASE WHEN s LIKE 'a%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS m FROM t ORDER BY id
duckdb.source: DuckDB pattern matching: ILIKE is used instead of LIKE to make the match case-insensitive.

cases.title: Adding a day and a month, a day difference and the month's end

spark.statement: SELECT date_add(d1, 1) AS next_day, add_months(d1, 1) AS next_month, datediff(d2, d1) AS days, last_day(d3) AS month_end FROM t
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL built-in functions date_add, add_months (add_months('2016-08-31', 1) is 2016-09-30), datediff and last_day.

databricks.statement: SELECT date_add(d1, 1) AS next_day, add_months(d1, 1) AS next_month, datediff(d2, d1) AS days, last_day(d3) AS month_end FROM t
databricks.source: Databricks SQL date_add, add_months (a day past the month's end becomes its last day), datediff and last_day functions.

snowflake.statement: SELECT DATEADD(day, 1, d1) AS next_day, DATEADD(month, 1, d1) AS next_month, DATEDIFF(day, d1, d2) AS days, LAST_DAY(d3) AS month_end FROM t
snowflake.source: Snowflake DATEADD (a DATE for day or larger parts; January 31 plus one month is the last day of February), DATEDIFF and LAST_DAY.

tsql.statement: SELECT DATEADD(day, 1, d1) AS next_day, DATEADD(month, 1, d1) AS next_month, DATEDIFF(day, d1, d2) AS days, EOMONTH(d3) AS month_end FROM t
tsql.source: T-SQL DATEADD (the date's own type; a day missing from the result month gives that month's last day), DATEDIFF and EOMONTH.

duckdb.statement: SELECT d1 + INTERVAL 1 DAY AS next_day, d1 + INTERVAL 1 MONTH AS next_month, date_diff('day', d1, d2) AS days, last_day(d3) AS month_end FROM t
duckdb.source: DuckDB date functions: date + INTERVAL returns a timestamp (DATE '1992-03-22' + INTERVAL 5 DAY is 1992-03-27 00:00:00), date_diff counts part boundaries, last_day.
duckdb.note: The page doesn't say what adding a month to January 31 gives; the last day of February is assumed.

cases.title: Day-of-week numbers and the first day of a week

spark.statement: SELECT dayofweek(d) AS dow, date_trunc('WEEK', d) AS wk FROM t
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL built-in functions: dayofweek (1 = Sunday ... 7 = Saturday); date_trunc returns a timestamp, WEEK truncates to the Monday.

databricks.statement: SELECT dayofweek(d) AS dow, date_trunc('WEEK', d) AS wk FROM t
databricks.source: Databricks SQL dayofweek (INTEGER, 1 = Sunday) and date_trunc (a TIMESTAMP, WEEK is the Monday).

snowflake.statement: SELECT DAYOFWEEK(d) AS dow, DATE_TRUNC('WEEK', d) AS wk FROM t
snowflake.source: Snowflake date and time functions: with WEEK_START 0 (the default) DAYOFWEEK is 0 (Sunday) to 6 (Saturday) and DATE_TRUNC to WEEK starts on Monday; DATE_TRUNC keeps its input's type.

tsql.statement: SELECT DATEPART(weekday, d) AS dow, DATETRUNC(week, d) AS wk FROM t
tsql.source: T-SQL DATEPART and DATETRUNC: weekday and week depend on @@DATEFIRST, 7 (Sunday) for U.S. English; DATETRUNC returns its input's type.
tsql.note: Assumes the default U.S. English language setting.

duckdb.statement: SELECT dayofweek(d) AS dow, date_trunc('week', d) AS wk FROM t
duckdb.source: DuckDB date part functions: dayofweek (Sunday = 0, Saturday = 6); date functions: date_trunc always returns a TIMESTAMP.
duckdb.note: The pages don't say which day date_trunc's week starts on; Monday (ISO) is assumed.

cases.title: Casting text that isn't a number to an integer

spark.statement: SELECT CAST(s AS INT) AS i FROM t
spark.source: Apache Spark ANSI compliance: with spark.sql.ansi.enabled false (Spark 3.5's default, as Fabric runs), CAST('a' AS INT) is NULL.

databricks.statement: SELECT CAST(s AS INT) AS i FROM t
databricks.source: Databricks SQL cast function and ANSI_MODE: invalid input raises CAST_INVALID_INPUT (cast('a' AS INTEGER) is an error with ANSI mode on, the default).

snowflake.statement: SELECT CAST(s AS INT) AS i FROM t
snowflake.source: Snowflake data type conversion: the VARCHAR value 'xyz' can't be converted to a numeric value.

tsql.statement: SELECT CAST(s AS int) AS i FROM t
tsql.source: T-SQL CAST and CONVERT: the Database Engine returns an error when converting nonnumeric varchar data to int.

duckdb.statement: SELECT CAST(s AS INTEGER) AS i FROM t
duckdb.source: DuckDB casting: CAST('hello' AS INTEGER) raises a Conversion Error; TRY_CAST gives NULL.

cases.title: Casting a double to an integer: truncate or round

spark.statement: SELECT id, CAST(x AS INT) AS i FROM t ORDER BY id
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL CAST.
spark.note: Spark's reference doesn't say whether a fractional value is truncated or rounded; Databricks documents truncation.

databricks.statement: SELECT id, CAST(x AS INT) AS i FROM t ORDER BY id
databricks.source: Databricks SQL cast function: to an integral type the result is truncated to a whole number (cast(-5.6 AS INT) is -5).

snowflake.statement: SELECT id, CAST(x AS INT) AS i FROM t ORDER BY id
snowflake.source: Snowflake data type conversion: converting a FLOAT value to an INTEGER value rounds the value.

tsql.statement: SELECT id, CAST(x AS int) AS i FROM t ORDER BY id
tsql.source: T-SQL CAST and CONVERT: float to int truncates (CAST(-10.6496 AS INT) is -10).

duckdb.statement: SELECT id, CAST(x AS INTEGER) AS i FROM t ORDER BY id
duckdb.source: DuckDB typecasting and numeric types: a fractional number cast to an integral type is rounded (CAST(-1.7 AS INTEGER) is -2).

cases.title: Casting text to a boolean

spark.statement: SELECT id, CAST(s AS BOOLEAN) AS b FROM t ORDER BY id
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL CAST.
spark.note: Spark's reference doesn't list the strings a boolean cast accepts; the list Databricks documents is assumed.

databricks.statement: SELECT id, CAST(s AS BOOLEAN) AS b FROM t ORDER BY id
databricks.source: Databricks SQL cast function: 'T', 'TRUE', 'Y', 'YES', '1' are true and 'F', 'FALSE', 'N', 'NO', '0' false, ignoring case.

snowflake.statement: SELECT id, TO_BOOLEAN(s) AS b FROM t ORDER BY id
snowflake.source: Snowflake TO_BOOLEAN: 'true', 't', 'yes', 'y', 'on', '1' are TRUE and 'false', 'f', 'no', 'n', 'off', '0' FALSE, ignoring case.

tsql.statement: SELECT id, CAST(s AS bit) AS b FROM t WHERE id < 3 ORDER BY id
tsql.source: T-SQL bit: the string values TRUE and FALSE can be converted to bit values, 1 and 0.
tsql.note: Row 3 ('yes') is left out: the page doesn't say what other strings give.

duckdb.statement: SELECT id, CAST(s AS BOOLEAN) AS b FROM t WHERE id < 3 ORDER BY id
duckdb.source: DuckDB typecasting: VARCHAR to BOOLEAN is an explicit cast.
duckdb.note: DuckDB's pages don't list the strings that cast to a boolean; 'true' and 'false' in any case are assumed. Row 3 ('yes') is left out.

cases.title: IN and NOT IN with a NULL in the list

spark.statement: SELECT id, CASE WHEN v IN (1, NULL) THEN 'T' WHEN NOT (v IN (1, NULL)) THEN 'F' ELSE 'U' END AS in_list, CASE WHEN v NOT IN (1, NULL) THEN 'T' WHEN NOT (v NOT IN (1, NULL)) THEN 'F' ELSE 'U' END AS not_in FROM t ORDER BY id
spark.source: Apache Spark NULL semantics: IN is UNKNOWN when the value is NULL or isn't found in a list holding NULL; NOT IN is always UNKNOWN when the list holds NULL.

databricks.statement: SELECT id, CASE WHEN v IN (1, NULL) THEN 'T' WHEN NOT (v IN (1, NULL)) THEN 'F' ELSE 'U' END AS in_list, CASE WHEN v NOT IN (1, NULL) THEN 'T' WHEN NOT (v NOT IN (1, NULL)) THEN 'F' ELSE 'U' END AS not_in FROM t ORDER BY id
databricks.source: Databricks SQL NULL semantics: IN and NOT IN with a NULL in the list.

snowflake.statement: SELECT id, CASE WHEN v IN (1, NULL) THEN 'T' WHEN NOT (v IN (1, NULL)) THEN 'F' ELSE 'U' END AS in_list, CASE WHEN v NOT IN (1, NULL) THEN 'T' WHEN NOT (v NOT IN (1, NULL)) THEN 'F' ELSE 'U' END AS not_in FROM t ORDER BY id
snowflake.source: Snowflake [ NOT ] IN: comparisons with NULL return NULL; NOT IN returns NULL if any value in the list is NULL; 1 IN (1, 2, NULL) is TRUE.

tsql.statement: SELECT id, CASE WHEN v IN (1, NULL) THEN 'T' WHEN NOT (v IN (1, NULL)) THEN 'F' ELSE 'U' END AS in_list, CASE WHEN v NOT IN (1, NULL) THEN 'T' WHEN NOT (v NOT IN (1, NULL)) THEN 'F' ELSE 'U' END AS not_in FROM t ORDER BY id
tsql.source: T-SQL IN: null values compared with the test expression using IN or NOT IN return UNKNOWN.
tsql.note: The page states the UNKNOWN case; that a match (1 IN (1, NULL)) is still TRUE is standard SQL.

duckdb.statement: SELECT id, CASE WHEN v IN (1, NULL) THEN 'T' WHEN NOT (v IN (1, NULL)) THEN 'F' ELSE 'U' END AS in_list, CASE WHEN v NOT IN (1, NULL) THEN 'T' WHEN NOT (v NOT IN (1, NULL)) THEN 'F' ELSE 'U' END AS not_in FROM t ORDER BY id
duckdb.source: DuckDB IN operator.
duckdb.note: DuckDB's page doesn't describe a NULL in the list; standard SQL three-valued logic is assumed.

cases.title: Adding 1 to the largest INT

spark.statement: SELECT a + 1 AS s FROM t
spark.source: Apache Spark ANSI compliance: with spark.sql.ansi.enabled false, whole-number arithmetic wraps as in Java (2147483647 + 1 is -2147483648).

databricks.statement: SELECT a + 1 AS s FROM t
databricks.source: Databricks SQL ANSI_MODE: with ANSI mode on (the default) arithmetic overflow is an error (100Y * 100Y).

snowflake.statement: SELECT a + 1 AS s FROM t
snowflake.source: Snowflake numeric data types: INT is a synonym for NUMBER(38,0), so there is no 32-bit limit.

tsql.statement: SELECT a + 1 AS s FROM t
tsql.source: T-SQL SET ANSI_WARNINGS: when ON, arithmetic overflow errors roll back the statement with an error; int + int is int.

duckdb.statement: SELECT a + 1 AS s FROM t
duckdb.source: DuckDB numeric types: storing a value outside the type's range is an error.
duckdb.note: The page states the error for storing values and for decimal arithmetic, not for INTEGER addition.

cases.title: The remainder of a negative number

spark.statement: SELECT id, a % b AS m, pmod(a, 3) AS p FROM t ORDER BY id
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL built-in functions: % is the remainder after expr1/expr2; pmod(-10, 3) is 2.
spark.note: The reference doesn't say which sign % gives for negative operands; the dividend's sign (as in Java) is assumed.

databricks.statement: SELECT id, a % b AS m, pmod(a, 3) AS p FROM t ORDER BY id
databricks.source: Databricks SQL % (percent sign) operator and pmod.

snowflake.statement: SELECT id, MOD(a, b) AS m FROM t ORDER BY id

tsql.statement: SELECT id, a % b AS m FROM t ORDER BY id

cases.title: ROUND of .5: half up, half away from zero or half even

spark.statement: SELECT id, round(x, 0) AS r, bround(x, 0) AS b FROM t ORDER BY id
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL built-in functions: round uses HALF_UP (round(2.5, 0) is 3), bround uses HALF_EVEN (bround(2.5, 0) is 2).
spark.note: -2.5 to -3 reads HALF_UP as Java's RoundingMode (away from zero); the reference shows positive values only.

databricks.statement: SELECT id, round(x, 0) AS r, bround(x, 0) AS b FROM t ORDER BY id
databricks.source: Databricks SQL round (HALF_UP; a DECIMAL keeps the smaller scale) and bround (HALF_EVEN): round(2.5, 0) is 3, bround(2.5, 0) is 2, both give 4 for 3.5.
databricks.note: -2.5 to -3 reads HALF_UP as away from zero; the page shows positive values only.

snowflake.statement: SELECT id, ROUND(x, 0) AS r, ROUND(x, 0, 'HALF_TO_EVEN') AS b FROM t ORDER BY id
snowflake.source: Snowflake ROUND: the default rounding mode is HALF_AWAY_FROM_ZERO (2.5 is 3, -2.5 is -3); HALF_TO_EVEN gives 2 and -2.

tsql.statement: SELECT id, ROUND(x, 0) AS r FROM t ORDER BY id
tsql.source: T-SQL ROUND breaks ties by rounding half away from zero; decimal(p, s) input returns decimal(p, s). T-SQL has no half-even ROUND.

duckdb.statement: SELECT id, round(x, 0) AS r, round_even(x, 0) AS b FROM t ORDER BY id
duckdb.source: DuckDB numeric functions: round rounds exact halfway cases away from zero; round_even uses half to even.

cases.title: UNION removes duplicate rows, UNION ALL keeps them

spark.statement: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT v FROM t UNION SELECT v FROM t) u) AS n_union, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT v FROM t UNION ALL SELECT v FROM t) a) AS n_all
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL set operators: UNION is UNION DISTINCT by default; UNION ALL keeps duplicates.

databricks.statement: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT v FROM t UNION SELECT v FROM t) u) AS n_union, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT v FROM t UNION ALL SELECT v FROM t) a) AS n_all
databricks.source: Databricks SQL set operators: UNION without ALL removes duplicates.

snowflake.statement: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT v FROM t UNION SELECT v FROM t) u) AS n_union, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT v FROM t UNION ALL SELECT v FROM t) a) AS n_all
snowflake.source: Snowflake set operators: UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL doesn't.

tsql.statement: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT v FROM t UNION SELECT v FROM t) u) AS n_union, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT v FROM t UNION ALL SELECT v FROM t) a) AS n_all
tsql.source: T-SQL set operators UNION: UNION removes duplicates, UNION ALL keeps them. COUNT returns int.

duckdb.statement: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT v FROM t UNION SELECT v FROM t) u) AS n_union, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT v FROM t UNION ALL SELECT v FROM t) a) AS n_all
duckdb.source: DuckDB set operations: UNION removes duplicate rows, UNION ALL keeps them.

cases.title: LAG and LEAD with a default value

spark.statement: SELECT v, LAG(v, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY v) AS prev_v, LEAD(v, 1, -1) OVER (ORDER BY v) AS next_v FROM t ORDER BY v
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL window functions: lag and lead return default when there is no offset row.

databricks.statement: SELECT v, LAG(v, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY v) AS prev_v, LEAD(v, 1, -1) OVER (ORDER BY v) AS next_v FROM t ORDER BY v
databricks.source: Databricks SQL lag and lead analytic window functions: default is returned when there is no such row.

snowflake.statement: SELECT v, LAG(v, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY v) AS prev_v, LEAD(v, 1, -1) OVER (ORDER BY v) AS next_v FROM t ORDER BY v
snowflake.source: Snowflake LAG and LEAD: default is returned when the offset goes out of the window.

tsql.statement: SELECT v, LAG(v, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY v) AS prev_v, LEAD(v, 1, -1) OVER (ORDER BY v) AS next_v FROM t ORDER BY v

duckdb.statement: SELECT v, LAG(v, 1, 0) OVER (ORDER BY v) AS prev_v, LEAD(v, 1, -1) OVER (ORDER BY v) AS next_v FROM t ORDER BY v
duckdb.source: DuckDB window functions: lag(expr, offset, default) and lead(expr, offset, default).

cases.title: A running SUM with ties in the ORDER BY: the default frame

spark.statement: SELECT id, SUM(v) OVER (ORDER BY k) AS s FROM t ORDER BY id
spark.source: Apache Spark SQL window functions (SELECT ... OVER).
spark.note: The reference doesn't state the frame used when ORDER BY has no frame clause; RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (ties share a sum) is assumed.

databricks.statement: SELECT id, SUM(v) OVER (ORDER BY k) AS s FROM t ORDER BY id
databricks.source: Databricks SQL window functions and window frame clause.
databricks.note: The pages don't state the default frame; RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is assumed.

snowflake.statement: SELECT id, SUM(v) OVER (ORDER BY k) AS s FROM t ORDER BY id
snowflake.source: Snowflake window function syntax: with ORDER BY and no frame, SUM uses RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, so tied rows share a sum.

tsql.statement: SELECT id, SUM(v) OVER (ORDER BY k) AS s FROM t ORDER BY id
tsql.source: T-SQL OVER clause: with ORDER BY and no ROWS or RANGE, RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is the default frame.

duckdb.statement: SELECT id, SUM(v) OVER (ORDER BY k) AS s FROM t ORDER BY id
duckdb.source: DuckDB window functions: the default frame is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW when ORDER BY is present.

cases.title: Dividing by zero: an error or NULL

spark.statement: SELECT a / b AS q FROM t
spark.source: Apache Spark ANSI compliance (try_divide is / without the exception) and Databricks Runtime: with spark.sql.ansi.enabled false, / returns NULL for a zero divisor.
spark.note: Spark's own reference doesn't state the ANSI-off result of /; Databricks' / page does.

databricks.statement: SELECT a / b AS q FROM t
databricks.source: Databricks SQL / (slash sign) operator: if the divisor is 0, raises DIVIDE_BY_ZERO; ANSI_MODE: 1/0 is an error with ANSI mode on.

snowflake.statement: SELECT a / b AS q FROM t
snowflake.source: Snowflake DIV0: like the division operator but returns 0 rather than reporting an error; select 1/0 fails with Division by zero.

tsql.statement: SELECT a / b AS q FROM t
tsql.source: T-SQL SET ANSI_WARNINGS: when ON, divide-by-zero errors roll back the statement with an error message.

duckdb.statement: SELECT isinf(a / b) AS q FROM t
duckdb.source: DuckDB numeric functions: / is float division, and only // and % are listed as throwing on division by zero; configuration: ieee_floating_point_ops (default true) returns NAN/INF instead of errors/NULL.
duckdb.note: No page shows 1 / 0. error_on_division_by_zero (default true) says it throws instead of returning NULL, but the numeric page lists only // and % as throwing. isinf shows the value, since JSON has no infinity.
